The FAA administrator said he expects airlines to resume full schedules by the end of the weekend.

 What to do if your flight has been canceled or delayed
 By Maria Aguilar Prieto 
 A passenger looks at flight information displays showing cancellations, in the check-in area of Los Angeles International Airport, California, on November 14. 
 Apu Gomes/AFP/Getty Images 
 As travelers continue to feel the effects of Friday’s nationwide ground stop, here are some tips for those who may be affected.
 If your flight is canceled and you decide not to travel, you are entitled to a refund, Clint Henderson, managing editor at The Points Guy, explained. He also advised travelers to keep receipts of any expenses incurred as a result of delays or cancellations.
 “Keep really good records because there is a chance that the airlines, even the government, could compensate you,” Henderson told CNN’s Kasie Hunt.
 Those who booked their trips with credit cards that offer travel protection benefits should also review their card’s policies to see what coverage might be available.
 For those who absolutely must travel, Henderson recommended looking into alternative plans as soon as disruptions begin.
 “If I start to see things going wrong, I have a plan B and a plan C already in mind,” Henderson said.
 Travelers might also have better luck rebooking flights through their airline’s app or by calling an international customer service number to avoid long waits, Henderson added.

 CNN talks to couple stuck in LA airport after 54th anniversary cruise 
 3:10
 Everything was going smoothly yesterday for Alan and Billie Jean Paul, fresh off a cruise to celebrate their 54th anniversary and about to fly back home to Texas. Then, with their plane waiting on the tarmac, the sign at their gate changed to read “Canceled.”
 “That was it. Total chaos,” Alan told CNN’s Leigh Waldman in the Los Angeles International Airport, where the couple worried they might’ve been stuck overnight after the Federal Aviation Administration’s nationwide ground stop went into effect.
 The Pauls were luckier than others , though, and managed to book a rental car and hotel room — which was over an hour away because everything close by had already been booked, Billie Jean said. But they had to pay much more than they expected because the price of both spiked as soon as flights got canceled.
 “Absolutely price gouging,” she said. “No doubt about it.”
 The couple is hoping to get on a flight out of Los Angeles today, but they are going to miss a high school class reunion at home because of the cancellations.
 “We’re never going to forget Friday the 13th, 2026,” Billie Jean said.

 Criticism of contractor over ground stop echoes similar outage in 2009, analyst says
 By Emma Tucker 
 As questions mount over what caused the communication outages that forced the nationwide ground stop yesterday, a former FAA safety inspector pointed to another outage in 2009 that similarly grounded hundreds of flights and caused thousands of delays.
 First, some context: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has criticized L3Harris , which was doing upgrade work on a dated system, over the communication outages. Duffy said there could have been mistakes made during the procedure, which involved replacing a copper wire with fiber. But Duffy also said it’s unclear whether there was a contractor error or faulty equipment during the switch, which will be part of the investigation into the outage.
 In a statement to CNN today, L3Harris said it is working with the Federal Aviation Administration to investigate the incident.
 Echoes of the past: L3Harris may have repeated the same mistakes it was accused of making in 2009 by the Office of Inspector General, according to David Soucie, former FAA safety inspector and CNN safety analyst. The major telecommunications outage in 2009 affected 129 air traffic control centers, according to the OIG.
 An OIG report in 2010 described how L3Harris was similarly replacing copper wires with fiber before that outage.
 Those air traffic control centers “went down at that time in 2009 for exactly the same reason it did this time,” said Soucie, who was the FAA’s contracting technical representative at the time.
 “What they were faulted with is that they didn’t have any systems in place to test the system before they implemented it,” he said of L3Harris.
 The OIG report said the cause of the 2009 outage stemmed from “errors introduced into the Harris network maintenance and network monitoring processes,” and included recommendations to prevent a similar outage reoccurring.
 “It’s just impossible to me to think that after learning that lesson in 2009, that Harris would come back in — the same contractor — and do exactly the same thing without the precautions in place,” Soucie said. “When this started to go bad, the orders from the FAA say that you have to have monitors in place to stop it from propagating itself. It did not do that. They did not follow that protocol, and that’s where we find ourselves in the place we are right now today.”

 Pilot union president says crews are working to get back on track safely
 By Dalia Faheid 
 Capt. Jason Ambrosi, a Delta Air Lines pilot and president of the Air Line Pilots Association, says the nationwide ground stop has been frustrating for “mission-oriented” crews, but they can “only fly so many hours in a day.”
 “We want to get them to their destinations as on-time as possible,” he told CNN today, while also maintaining safety standards and adhering to flight and duty time rules.
 The Federal Aviation Administration oversees around 50,000 flights daily. FAA regulations require pilots to get a minimum of 10 consecutive hours of rest before working, which must include at least 8 uninterrupted hours.
 “Now (we) are having longer days. We’re not able to finish the mission. And many times, as you’re seeing during this rebuilding process, crews are timing out, and we’re having to follow the regulatory requirements on rest and schedule,” Ambrosi said.
 Maximum flight duty periods are around 14 hours, but if unexpected delays happen, the pilots’ work time can be extended by up to two hours.
 That’s not always enough time to resolve an issue, and “we find ourselves in a situation where we just can’t go, and then the airline is forced to find a crew to replace us if possible,” Ambrosi said.
 Just as travelers were stranded at airports last night, crews were stuck trying to find hotels and other accommodations during lengthy delays, the union head said.
 Ambrosi said pilots remain committed to keeping passengers safe as airlines undergo the “lengthy process of rebuilding the schedule.”

 Trump has discussed air traffic control overhaul with GOP senator for months, source says
 By Kit Maher 
 Sen. Eric Schmitt R-Mo, speaks at Capitol Hill, on Sept. 29. 
 Manuel Balce Ceneta/AP/File 
 Republican Sen. Eric Schmitt has spoken to President Donald Trump several times over the past few months about legislation to modernize air traffic control, airport towers, terminals and other critical infrastructure, a source familiar with the matter said.
 They had a phone call Friday night after the nationwide ground stop, as CNN reported.
 Schmitt, who serves on the Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee, introduced the Modern Skies Act in September, which would provide $30 billion in additional federal funding to update the nation’s aviation infrastructure. He is pushing for it to be included in reconciliation so the funding can pass sooner. Republican Rep. Tracey Mann also introduced a companion bill in the House.
 The White House and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy helped draft the legislation, the source said. And in all the conversations Schmitt and Trump have had over the legislation, the president was extremely engaged and supportive of getting it done, the source added.
 The Trump administration sent a letter to Congress Friday morning, hours before the ground stop, asking for the $30 billion in additional funding, the source said. The letter from director of the Office of Management and Budget, Russ Vought, and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy was sent to leadership on the Senate and House Appropriations Committees. A copy that CNN obtained was dated November 12.
 The source said that the timing was a coincidence; the letter had been done all week but it needed certain approvals before being sent.
 On September 28 at a press conference promoting the legislation at DCA alongside Duffy, Schmitt said, “My intention is for this to be a very bipartisan effort to solve some of the problems that the traveling public and our country faces,” stressing the need for an “advanced and modern system.”

 More than 5,000 flights in the US canceled today — but there are signs of improvement
 By Emma Tucker and Aleena Fayaz 
 People check a flight information display board at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Virginia on Friday. 
 Li Rui/Xinhua/Getty Images 
 More than 5,000 flights within, into or out of the United States have been canceled for Saturday, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium.
 The 5,000 cancellations amount to nearly a quarter of all scheduled US departures.
 As of 3:30 p.m. ET, Delta Air Lines canceled 27% of its flights, American Airlines canceled 26% of its flights, and United Airlines canceled 25% of its flights. American leads with 1,527 cancellations, though JetBlue has canceled a staggering 44% of its schedule.
 There is some good news: Cirium said that while cancellations are comparatively high, the airlines are slowly improving with increasingly on-time arrivals.
 As Americans outlook their travel plans for tomorrow, data shows only 86 cancellations for Sunday thus far, which is in line with FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford’s prediction that a full recovery of flights will be achieved by the end of the day Sunday.

 CNN speaks to traveler in LAX trying to make it to Australia for a cruise 
 1:20
 Flying to Australia for a month-long cruise had long been a bucket-list item for Stephen Walter and his wife. But getting stranded at airports in Washington, DC, and then Los Angeles amid the nationwide ground stop has him considering whether it might be easier to just call it off and head back home.
 “It’s tempting. Really, it really is,” Walter told CNN’s Leigh Waldman. “It’s only two days out of a month, but still, it’s like, I just want to be there.”
 After the ground stop delayed their flight out of DC for several hours, Walter and his wife made it to LA, but missed their connecting flight to Australia. Now, the couple is going to miss their cruise boat leaving from Sydney tomorrow, so they’ll have to get on another flight once in Sydney and try to catch the ship in Brisbane, Walter said.
 To make matters worse, the couple’s bags never made it onto their plane from DC. Now they’re waiting near baggage claims in hopes they’ll arrive on another plane soon.
 “It’s been a nightmare,” Walter said.

 No active ground stops, but several cities face staffing concerns, FAA says
 By Pete Muntean 
 The Washington Monument is seen in the distance as passengers wait at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Virginia, on Saturday. 
 Aaron Schwartz/AFP/Getty Images 
 The FAA’s latest nationwide operations plan released this afternoon lists no active ground stops or ground delays.
 Weather may cause a potential ground stop or delay in Seattle after 5 p.m. ET, the FAA flagged. Las Vegas, Chicago, Nashville, Atlanta and Jacksonville also had staffing constraints, according to the plan.
 There are no indications in the plan of any lingering technical issues from yesterday’s nationwide meltdown. The air traffic control system appears to be back to normal — but the bigger problem now is airlines getting their planes and crews back into position.

 Operations back to normal at world's busiest airport
 By Ryan Young and Aleena Fayaz 
 Operations have mostly returned to normal at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, the airport’s communications department tells CNN.
 “Airport operations are normal. However, we are still encouraging passengers to check with their airlines before heading to the airport to make sure their flight is departing as scheduled,” the airport’s communications department tells CNN.
 Wait times at airport security are below six minutes at all gates. Despite ticket counters experiencing backups, the congestion is nowhere close to last night, according to the airport’s communication department.
 Boasting the title of world’s busiest airport with more than two thousand arrivals and departures daily, Hartsfield-Jackson averages almost 300,000 passengers per day.

 Johnson "working on" plan to revamp aviation systems. It’s unclear how Congress would fund it
 By Ellis Kim and Ted Barrett 
 House Speaker Mike Johnson speaks during a press conference on Tuesday in Washington, DC. 
 Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images 
 House Speaker Mike Johnson said Saturday he was “working on” a plan for Congress to pass funding to revamp the nation’s aviation systems, but he left unclear exactly how that spending would pass.
 “I’m here in D.C. this weekend working on that,” Johnson said during an appearance on Fox News . “We were working on an aggressive legislative package to finish out the year strong, run through the tape… and this will be added to that.”
 In June 2025, Congress approved $12.5 billion to update air traffic control systems as part of President Donald Trump’s massive spending and policy bill. But Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has repeatedly implored Congress to pass more funding, to the tune of $30 billion, to complete an overhaul of the nation’s air traffic systems. He doubled down on that ask Friday night and called for $50 billion.
 It was not immediately clear to congressional aides how leaders will pass new funding. Currently, appropriators are negotiating a government funding deal ahead of a December 11 deadline. Senate leadership aides in each party did not immediately respond to questions about the path forward in that chamber.
 In one sign that Duffy may not get the money as smoothly as he would like, Democratic Sen. Brian Schatz of Hawaii said in a post on X that ICE has an extra $60 billion this year and that some of it should be redirected to the FAA. That’s an idea the administration is not likely to back. Schatz is a member of the influential Senate Appropriations Committee and is expected to be the second ranking member in the Democratic leadership next Congress.
 Also, Duffy’s public push for $50 billion to revamp the FAA was seen as bad form by some who thought it was too political.
 “Honestly, I felt like Duffy sort of missed his moment because by doing that yesterday, I think you’re going to see a lot of skepticism on the Hill because of the political use of the money ask,” Juliette Kayyem, a former assistant secretary at DHS and a CNN analyst, told CNN’s Pamela Brown Saturday.
 Republican Sen. Eric Schmitt is also pushing for passage of his bill, the Modern Skies Act , which would invest $30 billion in modernizing the nation’s aviation system. The Missouri senator spoke with Trump on Friday, and has also spoken with Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on the topic.
 Johnson suggested Saturday his focus will be finding the new cash, rather than investigating the failures that led to Friday’s nationwide ground stop.
 Asked about potential legislative action or hearings, he told Fox News: “I’m sure some of our committees of jurisdiction will be engaged. You know, Homeland Security is involved in this, and other committees as well, but we don’t really need any investigation to understand. We need further investment.”
 “I mean some of this equipment dates back to the ’80s, so it’s got to be updated, and that’s our responsibility. We’re going to work to get it done,” he added.

 Trump receiving "constant updates" on air travel situation, though he hasn't commented
 By Molly English 
 President Donald Trump in Rock Hill, South Carolina, on October 29. 
 Andrew Harnik/Getty Images 
 President Donald Trump is receiving “constant updates” on the air travel situation after Friday’s widespread air traffic control communication outages and the FAA ground stop, according to a White House official.
 Trump still has not spoken publicly or posted on Truth Social about the airspace meltdown, instead firing off unrelated missives about plans to revitalize Hollywood and criticisms of California Gov. Gavin Newsom.
 The White House called a travel and photo “lid” just before noon on Saturday, meaning Trump is not expected to make any movements or appearances for the rest of the day.

 Contractor L3Harris says it's supporting FAA in investigating cause of ground stop
 By René Marsh and Kaanita Iyer 
 L3Harris — the contractor that handled the procedure of replacing a copper wire with fiber, which likely caused the nationwide ground stop yesterday — said in a statement to CNN today that it is working with the Federal Aviation Administration to investigate the incident.
 “L3Harris has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA,” the defense contractor said in the statement. “We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel. L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”
 At a news conference earlier today, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy criticized L3Harris, though he said it’s unclear whether there was a contractor error or faulty equipment during the switch.
 “Which begs the question for us: What did L3Harris do? Did they make mistakes yesterday?” Duffy told reporters. “They own this network. They’re our prime contractor. I can’t go somewhere else. They own it. Or was it a faulty router? And we’re going to find that out. And frankly, we’re going to hold people accountable.”

 What airlines are telling passengers about today's persistent delays
 By Alexandra Skores , Pete Muntean and Sydney Bishop
 American Airlines planes sit on the tarmac at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Virginia on Saturday. 
 Tom Brenner/AP 
 Major US carriers are warning passengers that flight delays will continue as they deal with the backlog caused by yesterday’s rare nationwide ground stop.
 Here’s what airlines have told passengers in recent updates: 
 American Airlines: The carrier is implementing fare caps, has added 1,750 seats through extra flights today, and is offering crews premium pay for certain flights as it scrambles to recover from Friday’s disruption.
 “Our teams worked through the night to rebuild the schedule and reposition aircraft and crews. We continue to recover today, though additional delays and cancellations are expected,” the carrier wrote.
 American canceled 1,240 of its flights yesterday, the most of any airline, according to FlightAware . Many passengers are trying to resume their travel on rebooked itineraries today.
 Delta: The airline encouraged customers to move their flights to Monday or later as it continues to restore operations.
 “Delta will provide customers with as much notice as possible about changes to flight schedules. When a cancellation does occur, Delta will automatically rebook customers to the next best itinerary,” the company said in an update.
 Delta canceled the second-most flights Friday, with 1,169, creating a backlog of its own.
 Southwest: The airline is offering a waiver to allow customers to cancel their flights or rebook them at a later date without penalty, it said this morning.
 “Although we are in position to operate a robust schedule, we ask Customers to be patient as we work to accommodate those who were unable to complete their travel on Friday,” the company said.
 The carrier had the third-most cancellations yesterday at 1,167, according to FlightAware.

 Travel chaos lingers as officials investigate yesterday’s ground stop. Catch up here
 By Tori B. Powell 
 Travelers wait in a terminal at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Virginia on Saturday. 
 Aaron Schwartz/AFP/Getty Images 
 Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy this morning took questions and talked more about the circumstances that led to yesterday’s rare nationwide ground stop.
 But question remain as it’s still unclear whether faulty equipment or contractor error was at the root of the telecommunication outages that forced the ground stop.
 Catch up on the latest: 
 What happened: The system outage was caused by an equipment error , said Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford at today’s news conference alongside Duffy. He and Duffy both emphasized again today that the outages do not appear to be caused by a cyberattack. And Duffy told reporters that the SMART system the department had deployed a few months ago was not responsible for the outages. Also, Bedford said that no air traffic control en route centers “actually went dark” yesterday, though as many as 17 of 22 facilities were affected.
 Pointing fingers: Duffy said today there could have been “mistakes made” by L3Harris — the defense contractor behind America’s leading air traffic surveillance system — during a routine procedure that led to the nationwide ground stop, adding that people will be held “accountable.” He said he is currently “stuck” with L3Harris.
 More explanations: Duffy said the upgrades made yesterday were necessary and that the nature of the switchover “was a remote location” and wasn’t expected to cause any malfunction. Bedford apologized to impacted travelers but maintained that “we did it for the right reasons.”
 Looking ahead: Bedford said he’s “ very, very confident that the system is operating as safe today as it was two weeks ago,” and Duffy said earlier today on X “it is safe to fly.” But there is still some copper wiring connecting FAA systems across the country that needs to be replaced , and officials are working to identify where it is, according to the transportation secretary. He called on Congress for more investments into the aviation industry.
 Lingering travel chaos: Long lines, frustrated travelers and reshuffled plans prevail at airports across the country even after the ground stop was lifted and air traffic control centers resumed normal operations . As of this afternoon, more than 4,500 flights have been cancelled and 4,600 flights have been delayed within, into or out of the country today so far, according to the aviation tracking platform FlightAware . And an incoming storm moving into the Pacific Northwest could complicate flight operations even further in the region this evening.

 Passengers express frustrations in their journey to get home after nationwide ground stop

 John and Rosemary were on their way back home to Seattle from a trip to Fiji yesterday when the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop for all flights. Their flight from Los Angeles was canceled and then rebooked, and then “delayed, delayed, delayed, delayed, canceled, in that order,” John said.
 “By that time, it was too late to get a hotel, so we sat right here all night, and it will be until 7:45 this evening,” John told CNN’s Leigh Waldman at the Los Angeles International Airport.
 The couple were far from the only ones spending their night in the airport, Rosemary said, after tens of thousands of flights were canceled and delayed yesterday and today.
 “This has been very frustrating,” Rosemary said. “I’m very tired, John’s very tired, and there’s no place to sleep other than on the floor of the airport. And there are people everywhere sleeping, because where else are you going to go?”
 Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said today that either aging equipment or contractor error was at the root of telecommunication outages that forced the ground stop. John and Rosemary said it was frustrating that the infrastructure of such an important system hadn’t been properly maintained.
 “I wish we could blame someone, but I don’t know who to blame,” John said. He later added: “Well, maybe our tax dollars aren’t really always going where they should. That’s all I got to say about that.”

 A closer look at L3Harris, the tech firm behind the FAA’s communications system
 By Auzinea Bacon 
 L3Harris, the defense contractor behind America’s leading air traffic surveillance system, is under scrutiny following the Federal Aviation Administration’s ground stop and criticism from Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy .
 The FAA cited safety concerns related to a telecommunications outage for yesterday’s rare nationwide order. L3Harris manages the largest surveillance system, including more than 45,000 daily flights across the airspace system, and connects more than 4,400 facilities, according to the company.
 L3Harris, which was founded in 2019, says it is currently working on modernizing the administration’s technology, with just 70% of sites upgraded from “decades-old copper wire connections” to high-speed networks. It also operates the FAA’s Data Comm program, which manages air traffic.
 Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin have suggested updates to the FAA’s aging systems were behind the halt on flights, but Trump administration officials have yet to pinpoint whether contractor error or a faulty router was ultimately to blame.
 L3Harris has not yet responded to CNN’s requests for comment.
 “Our team’s deep knowledge of the U.S. national airspace allows us to upgrade systems without disrupting air traffic operations,” the company’s website says, adding that it coordinates with FAA staff “to ensure (air traffic) controllers have the connectivity they need.”
 The Florida-based company, which also works with the Department of Defense, was responsible for upgrading the Boeing 747 jet gifted to President Donald Trump from Qatar. Former CEO Christopher Kubasik said the company was “deeply honored” to work on the Air Force One plane.
 Kubasik was ousted from the role in August over conduct “not consistent” with company values, but wasn’t connected to L3Harris’ “financial reporting, controls, customer relationships or operational performance,” according to the company.
 Shares of L3Harris ( LHX ) fell 3.82% on Friday in after-hours trading.
